title: Understanding Harm
description: A six-lesson foundation course that helps parents and caregivers recognise harm, understand a child's experience, take accountability, repair relationships, and practise protective parenting.

reviewStatus.label: Production draft — not validated or approved
reviewStatus.learnerNotice: This educational course is a production draft. It does not replace personalised clinical, cultural, legal, or safeguarding advice.

audience.primary: Parents and caregivers referred for parenting support
audience.secondary: Parents and caregivers choosing to learn voluntarily
audience.delivery: Self-paced or supported by a practitioner

learningOutcomes: Define harm and recognise actions or omissions that can affect a child
Identify emotional, physical, relational, developmental, and cumulative harm
Describe possible impacts without diagnosing a child
Use accountability language without blame, excuses, or asking a child for reassurance
Choose practical repair steps that centre safety and the child's pace
Create a realistic protective parenting plan and support pathway

sections.title: What is harm?

content.title: Recognising impact, not labelling people
content.overview: Harm is an action, pattern, or omission that negatively affects a child's safety, wellbeing, development, relationships, or emotional health. This lesson focuses on observable behaviour and impact rather than labels.
content.psychoeducation: A parent can love a child and still use a response that causes harm. Learning to notice impact creates room for safer choices. Intent matters for understanding a situation, but it does not erase a child's experience.
learning_goals: Recognise when immediate safety takes priority
step_by_step: Pause and describe what happened without judgement.
Ask what the child may have seen, heard, felt, or needed.
Check emotional and physical safety before correcting behaviour.
Choose a calm next step and seek support when safety is uncertain.
parent_scripts: I can see that felt scary. Your safety matters more than finishing this argument.
I did not mean to frighten you, and I can see that my shouting did. I am going to lower my voice and give us space.
You do not have to make me feel better. I am responsible for what I do next.
practical_examples: A child is mocked whenever they cry. Repeated dismissal may cause emotional and relational harm.
A caregiver is overwhelmed and misses a child's basic supervision needs. Harm can occur through omission as well as action.
A parent notices rising anger, moves away safely, and asks another trusted adult for support before continuing.
reflection_questions: When I feel challenged, what changes first in my body, voice, or words?
What helps me pause before I respond?
Which trusted person or service can I contact if I am worried about safety?
practice_ideas: Use the pause, describe, safety-check, and next-step sequence once this week.
Write one short phrase that helps you slow down and keep it where you can see it.
content.closing_message: Recognising impact is a protective skill. It is not a verdict about your worth as a parent.

facilitator.openingScript: Welcome. We will talk about harm without asking you to disclose personal experiences. You may pass, pause, or use a fictional example at any time.
teachingPrompts: What is observable in this situation?
What might the child need first?
How can the adult reduce risk before discussing consequences?

feedback.strong: You centred the child's immediate safety and described impact without labelling the person.
feedback.developing: Look again at what the child may experience, even if the adult did not intend harm.
feedback.remediation: Review the difference between intent and impact, then retry with safety as the first priority.

activities.title: Impact lens
activities.instructions: Choose a fictional difficult moment. Describe what happened, what the child might experience, and one safer next step.
activities.completionPrompt: Name one action that would increase safety.

scenario.prompt: A child is highly distressed after an adult has shouted. What should the adult prioritise?
scenario.hint: Think about what the child needs before correction or explanation.

choices.text: Immediate punishment
choices.feedback: Punishment during high distress can increase fear and reduce the child's ability to listen.

choices.text: Emotional and physical safety
choices.feedback: Correct. Safety and regulation come before correction or problem-solving.

choices.text: Winning the argument
choices.feedback: Winning an argument does not address the child's safety or distress.

choices.text: Ignoring the behaviour
choices.feedback: Space may help when used safely, but ignoring distress without checking safety can leave the child unsupported.

quiz.hint: Harm can result from actions and omissions.

choices.text: Only an action that causes a visible injury
An action, pattern, or omission that negatively affects a child
Any time a child is unhappy with a limit

sections.homePractice: Notice one difficult moment this week. Record the trigger, your pause strategy, and the safe response you chose.

red_flags: A child or adult says they are in immediate danger
There is a threat of serious harm, violence, or self-harm
A child discloses abuse or neglect
when_to_escalate: Pause the lesson and use emergency or safeguarding pathways when danger is immediate.
Contact an appropriate qualified service or practitioner when safety is uncertain.
Follow applicable mandatory reporting and organisational procedures.

sections.title: Types and patterns of harm

content.title: Looking beyond a single incident
content.overview: Harm can be emotional, psychological, physical, relational, developmental, or connected to unmet care and supervision needs. Repeated lower-level experiences can also have a cumulative impact.
content.psychoeducation: Categories can help us notice patterns, but real experiences may overlap. The purpose is not to diagnose or investigate. It is to recognise concern, reduce risk, and involve qualified support when needed.
step_by_step: Record the specific behaviour or omission.
Notice frequency, intensity, duration, and context.
Consider possible impact without diagnosing.
Identify protective factors and the next safe support.
parent_scripts: I want to understand the pattern, not make excuses for it.
I can describe what happened without guessing what my child thinks.
If I am unsure about safety, I will ask for qualified help.
practical_examples: Repeatedly humiliating a child can affect self-worth and trust even when there is no physical injury.
Using a child to carry hostile messages between adults creates loyalty pressure and relational harm.
Unpredictable supervision may affect both physical safety and a child's sense of security.
reflection_questions: Which patterns are easiest for me to notice, and which are easier to minimise?
How can I record observations without labelling my child or myself?
practice_ideas: Use a neutral log: what happened, when, what came before, and what helped.
Identify one protective person, routine, or place that supports your family.
content.closing_message: Patterns become easier to change when they are described clearly and without shame.

facilitator.openingScript: This lesson uses fictional examples. You control what you share, and identifying a category is not the same as making a diagnosis.
teachingPrompts: What did the observer actually see or hear?
Is this a one-off event, a pattern, or unknown?
Which protective factor could reduce risk?

feedback.strong: You separated observation from assumption and noticed that types of harm can overlap.
feedback.developing: Try describing the behaviour and pattern before deciding what it means.
feedback.remediation: Review frequency, intensity, duration, and context, then identify one protective factor.

activities.title: Observe, assume, or protect
activities.instructions: Sort fictional statements into observable fact, assumption, or protective response.
activities.completionPrompt: Rewrite one assumption as a neutral observation.

scenario.prompt: A child is repeatedly told that their feelings are silly and should be hidden. What is the best interpretation?
scenario.hint: Consider the repeated relational and emotional impact.

choices.text: It always builds resilience
choices.feedback: Repeated dismissal can undermine emotional safety and help-seeking.

choices.text: It may contribute to emotional and relational harm
choices.feedback: Correct. The repeated pattern may affect trust, expression, and self-worth.

choices.text: It proves the child has a disorder
choices.feedback: The scenario does not support a diagnosis. Focus on observable behaviour and impact.

quiz.hint: Think about the effect of repeated experiences over time.

choices.text: The combined impact of repeated harmful experiences
Only one severe physical incident
A formal diagnosis made by an app

sections.homePractice: Use neutral language to record one recurring pressure point and one protective factor.

red_flags: Escalating threats, intimidation, or physical aggression
A child appears fearful of returning to a person or place
Basic care or supervision needs are not being met
when_to_escalate: Do not investigate a disclosure through repeated questioning.
Record the child's words accurately where required and seek qualified safeguarding guidance.
Use emergency services when there is immediate danger.

sections.title: Impact on children

content.title: Seeing the situation from the child's side
content.overview: Children may respond to stress through fight, flight, freeze, fawn, withdrawal, clinginess, aggression, sleep changes, or difficulty concentrating. These are possible signals, not proof of a cause or diagnosis.
content.psychoeducation: A child's behaviour often communicates an unmet need or an overwhelmed nervous system. Developmental stage, disability, culture, temperament, previous experiences, and current supports all shape how stress appears.
learning_goals: Describe possible child impacts without diagnosing
Choose connection and co-regulation before correction
step_by_step: Notice the child's cues and your own activation.
Reduce noise, demands, or proximity when helpful and safe.
Use few words and a calm tone.
Reconnect and problem-solve after regulation returns.
parent_scripts: Your body looks like it needs a pause. I am here.
You can tell me, draw it, point, or choose not to talk right now.
We will solve the problem after we are both calmer.
practical_examples: A school-age child becomes defiant during transitions. Predictable warnings and two safe choices reduce pressure.
A teenager withdraws after conflict. The caregiver checks safety, respects space, and offers a specific time to reconnect.
A young child becomes clingy after a frightening argument. Reassurance and consistent routines help restore predictability.
reflection_questions: What behaviours might I misread as deliberate disrespect?
How could age, disability, culture, or stress change what support is useful?
practice_ideas: Offer two accessible ways for a child to communicate a need.
content.closing_message: Curiosity about behaviour helps you respond to need while keeping clear, safe limits.

facilitator.openingScript: We will explore possible impacts without diagnosing children or asking you to interpret every behaviour as trauma.
teachingPrompts: What else could this behaviour communicate?
What expectation fits the child's developmental stage?
What would connection before correction look like here?

feedback.strong: You stayed curious, avoided diagnosis, and chose a developmentally appropriate response.
feedback.developing: Consider what the behaviour may communicate before treating it as deliberate defiance.
feedback.remediation: Choose one co-regulation step, then one clear limit for after the child is calmer.

activities.title: Child perspective
activities.instructions: Read a fictional situation and identify what the child may see, feel, need, and be able to do at their age.
activities.completionPrompt: Choose one connection step and one later boundary.

scenario.prompt: A child cannot answer questions while crying and breathing quickly. What is the most helpful first response?
scenario.hint: A highly activated child may not be ready for reasoning.

choices.text: Ask more questions until the child explains
Reduce demands, check safety, and co-regulate
choices.feedback: Correct. Help the child return to a safer, calmer state before problem-solving.

choices.text: Tell the child they are overreacting
choices.feedback: Dismissal may increase distress and reduce trust.

quiz.hint: Signals should guide support, not automatic conclusions.

choices.text: One behaviour proves a specific diagnosis
Behaviour may communicate stress, need, or limited regulation skills
Children should regulate exactly like adults

sections.homePractice: During one low-risk difficult moment, name the child's cue and try connection before correction.

red_flags: A child cannot be kept physically safe
A child reports fear, abuse, neglect, or violence
A caregiver feels unable to control an urge to harm
when_to_escalate: Move to immediate safety and contact emergency support when needed.
Pause educational coaching when clinical or safeguarding support is required.
Do not rely on the course to assess or manage acute risk.

sections.title: Accountability and responsibility

content.title: Owning behaviour without collapsing into shame
content.overview: Accountability means naming what you did, recognising impact, accepting responsibility, and following through on change. Shame says a person is beyond repair; accountability focuses on the next safer action.
content.psychoeducation: An accountable response does not include 'but you made me', pressure for forgiveness, or asking the child to comfort the adult. Context can explain a response without excusing it.
step_by_step: Name your action plainly.
Acknowledge the likely impact.
Take responsibility without a 'but'.
State the concrete change and support you will use.
Allow the child time and choice in reconnecting.
parent_scripts: I shouted. That was frightening and not okay.
You did not cause my reaction. I am responsible for how I respond.
Next time I will step away safely and call my support person before I continue.
practical_examples: Instead of 'I am sorry, but you would not listen,' say 'I shouted. That was not safe. I will use a pause next time.'
An adult accepts that trust may rebuild slowly and continues consistent safer behaviour.
A caregiver asks a practitioner for regulation support rather than promising change without a plan.
reflection_questions: Which accountability step is hardest for me?
What support makes follow-through more realistic?
practice_ideas: Rewrite one excuse as an accountable statement.
Choose one visible, repeatable behaviour change for the next week.
content.closing_message: Accountability is demonstrated through consistent action, not a perfect sentence.

facilitator.openingScript: Accountability is not humiliation. We will practise language that owns behaviour and protects the child from carrying the adult's emotions.
teachingPrompts: Where does this statement shift responsibility?
What specific action would show change?
How can the child keep choice and space?

feedback.strong: You named the behaviour, owned the impact, and committed to a specific change without demanding forgiveness.
feedback.developing: Remove the justification and make the next action more specific.
feedback.remediation: Use the pattern: I did; it affected; I am responsible; next time I will.

activities.title: From excuse to accountability
activities.instructions: Rewrite three fictional statements to remove blame, minimisation, and pressure for forgiveness.
activities.completionPrompt: Include one concrete support or behaviour change.

scenario.hint: Look for ownership without blame or pressure.

choices.text: I am sorry, but you made me lose my temper
choices.feedback: This shifts responsibility to the child.

choices.text: I shouted. That was not safe. You did not cause it. I will pause and get support next time
choices.feedback: Correct. This names the action, impact, responsibility, and change.

choices.text: I said sorry, so you need to forgive me now
choices.feedback: Forgiveness cannot be demanded, and repair may take time.

quiz.prompt: What is a key part of accountability?

choices.text: Explaining why the child caused the response
Taking responsibility and following through on safer behaviour
Obtaining immediate forgiveness

sections.homePractice: Use the four-part accountability pattern for a low-risk repair and note the action you followed through on.

red_flags: An apology is used to regain access, silence concern, or pressure a child
Violence or coercive behaviour is continuing
The adult cannot maintain a safe interaction
when_to_escalate: Do not use apology or course completion as evidence that risk has ended.
Seek specialist support for ongoing violence, coercion, or unsafe behaviour.
Respect safety plans, legal conditions, and professional directions.

sections.title: Repair and recovery

content.title: Rebuilding trust through safe repetition
content.overview: Repair is the ongoing process of restoring emotional and physical safety after harm. It includes accountability, changed behaviour, respect for boundaries, and patience with the child's response.
content.psychoeducation: A child may not be ready to talk, hug, or forgive. Repair cannot require closeness. Trust is rebuilt through repeated safe experiences and appropriate support, not promises alone.
learning_goals: Identify the parts of a safe repair
Respect a child's pace and boundaries
step_by_step: Make sure the harmful behaviour has stopped.
Acknowledge the impact and take responsibility.
Ask what would help without making the child responsible for the plan.
Respect space, boundaries, and existing safety arrangements.
Repeat the safer behaviour and review support needs.
parent_scripts: You do not have to talk or hug me. I will respect your space.
I am working on changing what I do, not asking you to forget what happened.
I will keep following the safety plan and show change over time.
practical_examples: A parent keeps their voice steady during repeated stressful routines rather than expecting one apology to restore trust.
A child declines physical affection, and the caregiver accepts the boundary without sulking or pressure.
A caregiver reviews setbacks with a practitioner and strengthens the support plan.
reflection_questions: Have I confused apology with completed repair?
Which boundary do I need to respect consistently?
What will help me sustain change when stress returns?
practice_ideas: Create a seven-day repair plan with one small repeated action.
Identify how you will respond safely if the child does not want to reconnect yet.
content.closing_message: Repair is measured by safety, consistency, and respect over time.

facilitator.openingScript: Repair does not guarantee reconciliation or access. This lesson focuses on the adult's safe actions and respect for the child's boundaries.
teachingPrompts: Where does the child retain choice?
What repeatable action would build predictability?

feedback.strong: You treated repair as consistent safe action and preserved the child's boundaries.
feedback.developing: Move the focus away from receiving forgiveness and toward sustained behaviour change.
feedback.remediation: Choose one boundary to respect and one action you can repeat reliably.

activities.title: Seven-day repair plan
activities.instructions: Choose one safe, observable action to repeat, one boundary to respect, and one support to use.
activities.completionPrompt: Describe how you will respond if the child wants space.

scenario.prompt: After an apology, a child does not want a hug. What is the safest response?
scenario.hint: Repair preserves the child's bodily autonomy.

choices.text: Insist because the apology should be accepted
choices.feedback: This pressures the child and undermines their boundary.

choices.text: Respect the boundary and continue showing safe change
choices.feedback: Correct. The child controls physical affection and may need time.

choices.text: Withdraw support until the child forgives
choices.feedback: Withholding support adds pressure and does not demonstrate repair.

quiz.hint: Look for sustained action rather than a single promise.

choices.text: One emotional apology
Repeated safe behaviour, accountability, and respect for boundaries
Asking the child to reassure the adult

sections.homePractice: Complete your seven-day repair action and record what helped you follow through.

red_flags: Repair language is used to bypass a safety plan or legal condition
The child is pressured to forgive, reconnect, or provide affection
Harmful behaviour continues while apologies repeat
when_to_escalate: Keep existing safety arrangements in place.
Seek practitioner or specialist review when repair attempts are unsafe or coercive.
Do not interpret course participation as evidence that contact or placement should change.

sections.title: Protective parenting plan

content.title: Turning learning into a supportable plan
content.overview: Protective parenting combines early warning signs, regulation strategies, child-centred responses, clear boundaries, practical supports, and escalation steps. A useful plan is specific enough to use under stress.
content.psychoeducation: There is no single programme or strategy that fits every family, population, culture, disability, or outcome. Plans should be personalised, reviewed with appropriate support, and changed when they are not improving safety.
learning_goals: Identify personal warning signs and protective factors
Know when to seek urgent or specialist help
Review progress without treating a score as proof of safety
step_by_step: Name your early warning signs.
Choose a safe pause action.
Identify the child's immediate support needs.
List trusted people and professional supports.
Write urgent escalation steps.
Set a date to review what is and is not working.
parent_scripts: I am getting too activated to respond safely. I am taking a safe pause now.
You are not responsible for calming me. I am contacting my support person.
This plan needs to change because it is not keeping us safe enough.
practical_examples: A caregiver recognises clenched hands and a raised voice as early warning signs and uses a planned handover.
A parent adapts verbal instructions for a child who communicates more easily through pictures.
A family reviews the plan with a culturally appropriate service rather than assuming one strategy fits.
reflection_questions: What are my earliest reliable warning signs?
Which support can I realistically contact outside business hours?
How will I know this plan needs review?
practice_ideas: Save your support contacts where they are accessible under stress.
Rehearse the safe pause sequence during a calm moment.
Review the plan with a trusted practitioner or support person.
content.closing_message: A protective plan is a living support tool. Using help early is a strength.

facilitator.openingScript: The goal is a plan you can use, not a perfect answer. Choose options that fit your family, culture, access needs, and current safety arrangements.
teachingPrompts: Can this step be used under stress?
Who is responsible for each action?
What happens if the first support is unavailable?
What signals mean the plan needs urgent review?

feedback.strong: Your plan identifies early signs, safe actions, support people, and clear escalation steps.
feedback.developing: Make the plan more specific by naming who, when, and what happens if the first option fails.
feedback.remediation: Start with one early warning sign, one safe pause, one support contact, and one urgent escalation step.

activities.title: My protective parenting plan
activities.instructions: Create a plan with warning signs, pause actions, child supports, trusted contacts, professional supports, urgent escalation steps, and a review date.
activities.completionPrompt: Confirm that the child is not responsible for managing the adult's safety plan.

scenario.prompt: A parent's usual calming strategy is not working and they fear they may act unsafely. What should they do?
scenario.hint: A plan needs a next level of support.

choices.text: Keep pushing through alone
choices.feedback: Continuing without support may increase risk.

choices.text: Use the escalation plan, create distance safely, and contact urgent support
choices.feedback: Correct. Escalating support early protects both the child and the adult.

choices.text: Ask the child to calm the parent
choices.feedback: Children should not be responsible for regulating or protecting an adult.

quiz.prompt: Which feature makes a protective plan more usable?
quiz.hint: A plan should still work when the first option is unavailable.

choices.text: Specific steps, named supports, backup options, and review points
A promise to never struggle again
Making the child responsible for monitoring the adult

sections.homePractice: Rehearse the safe pause and contact sequence once while calm, then update anything that is unclear.

red_flags: The adult fears they may harm a child, themselves, or another person
There is immediate danger, violence, weapon access, or a serious threat
No available adult can maintain the child's immediate safety
when_to_escalate: Contact emergency services for immediate danger.
Use crisis, family violence, child protection, or clinical pathways appropriate to the location and situation.
Notify the assigned practitioner through approved channels when it is safe and appropriate.

Course completion by itself

Withdraw support
